notes.meaning: Samson traveled deep into enemy territory to the Philistine city of Gaza. While there, he visited a prostitute instead of guarding his life and his calling. His choice showed how easily he gave in to his desires, walking right into spiritual and physical danger.

differ.view: Some say the words 'went in' do not have to mean sex. Staying at a prostitute's house may have been a way to enter the town without being noticed, like the spies at Rahab's house. This view admits most readers take it as sex.

notes.meaning: Word spread quickly among the people of Gaza that their greatest enemy was inside their city walls. The leaders shut the city gates and decided to wait quietly until morning to ambush him. They felt confident that he was trapped and could not get away.

Samson got up in the middle of the night and walked to the locked city gates. Using God-given strength, he tore out the heavy doors, the posts, and the locking bar, carrying them miles away up a hill toward Hebron. Even though Samson was living carelessly, God still gave him power to humiliate the Philistines.

Later on, Samson fell in love with a woman named Delilah who lived in the Sorek Valley. Samson allowed his feelings to guide him toward another dangerous romance. Delilah, however, did not return his affection and cared only for her own gain.

The five Philistine rulers saw an opportunity to finally stop Samson. They offered Delilah a massive fortune of eleven hundred silver coins each if she could uncover the secret of his strength. The rulers believed his power came from a hidden charm or magic secret rather than the true God.

Delilah asked Samson directly where his great strength came from and how he could be tied up securely. She disguised her dark plan as simple curiosity and playful affection. Samson stayed with her even though she openly asked how to overpower him.

Samson teased Delilah with a false answer instead of revealing his secret. He told her that seven fresh, unused bowstrings made of animal gut would make him as weak as an ordinary man. By mentioning the sacred number seven, he began to toy dangerously with his holy calling.

The Philistine lords quickly brought the fresh bowstrings to Delilah. She tied Samson up while he was resting, likely pretending it was just a playful game. Her actions proved right away that she was working with his enemies.

With Philistine men hidden in the next room ready to strike, Delilah shouted that the enemy had arrived. Samson instantly snapped the cords as easily as thread touching a fire. The Philistines stayed hidden, and Samson remained blind to the real danger in his home.

Delilah acted hurt and scolded Samson for mocking her with lies. She pressured him again to tell her the true way to bind him. Instead of running away from a trap, Samson continued to play along with her games.

Samson made up a second lie, claiming that brand-new ropes that had never been used for work would rob him of his strength. This sounded convincing because fresh ropes are strong, but it was another fiction. He continued to act as if his strength could never be lost.

Delilah bound Samson with the new ropes and called out the same warning as before. Once again, Samson easily broke the cords off his arms as if they were simple threads. He showed amazing physical power, yet he lacked the wisdom to leave a woman who kept trying to trap him.

Delilah complained a third time that Samson was making a fool of her. This time, Samson moved closer to the truth by mentioning his hair, which was plaited into seven braids. He told her that weaving his hair into a weaving loom would make him weak.

While Samson slept, Delilah wove his hair into the loom and fastened it firmly with a wooden peg. When she cried out that the Philistines were upon him, he awoke and ripped the pin and weaving frame right out of the floor. He escaped again, but he was getting dangerously close to surrendering his sacred sign.

Delilah challenged Samson's love, accusing him of holding back his heart from her. She claimed that true love would not hide secrets or mock her three times. She used emotional guilt to wear down his defenses.

Day after day, Delilah nagged and pleaded with Samson until he was completely exhausted and sick of life. His inner struggle between his romantic desire and his secret wore him out. Because he refused to walk away from temptation, his willpower finally broke.

Samson finally opened his entire heart and shared the truth. He explained that he was a Nazirite, someone set apart for God from birth, and a razor had never touched his head. His real strength did not live in the hair itself, but in his special relationship with God, of which his hair was the outward sign.

Delilah could tell from Samson's serious words that he had finally revealed his true secret. She sent an urgent message to the Philistine lords telling them to return one last time with the reward. The rulers came back, confident that Samson had finally fallen into their hands.

Delilah lulled Samson to sleep with his head resting on her lap. She then called a man to shave off the seven braids of his hair. As his sacred vow was broken, Samson's supernatural power left him, and Delilah began to overpower him.

When Delilah gave her familiar cry, Samson woke up expecting to break free just as he had done before. He did not realize that his vow was broken and the Lord had left him. Presuming on God's gifts without living in obedience brings sudden, tragic defeat.

The Philistines quickly grabbed the helpless Samson and gouged out his eyes so he could never fight them again. They dragged him to Gaza in heavy bronze chains and forced him to turn a heavy stone mill to grind flour in prison. The mighty champion of Israel was reduced to doing the work of a slave.

While he suffered in prison, Samson's hair slowly began to grow back. This quiet detail hinted that God had not completely abandoned him and that Samson was turning back to the Lord in his heart. It offered a ray of hope that God's purpose for Samson was not finished.

The Philistine leaders held a massive festival to make sacrifices to Dagon, their false god. They celebrated wildly, boasting that Dagon had handed their greatest enemy over to them. Samson's failure caused the enemies of Israel to mock the true God.

When the crowds saw the blind and chained Samson, they burst into cheers and praises for Dagon. They celebrated because Samson had ruined their crops and killed many of their warriors in past battles. Their joy was centered on thinking their idol was stronger than Israel's Lord.

As the crowd became drunken and festive, they demanded that Samson be brought out of prison to make sport for them. They forced him to stand between the main pillars so everyone could laugh at him and mock him. Cruelly humiliating God's servant only set the stage for their own destruction.

Samson spoke to the young boy who was leading him by the hand, asking to touch the pillars that supported the temple so he could rest against them. He wanted to feel exactly where the center of the building stood. The boy had no idea what Samson was planning.

The building was packed with all the Philistine rulers and citizens, and about three thousand men and women watched from the flat roof. They all looked down to watch Samson suffer and perform. The entire leadership of the Philistines was gathered in one crowded place.

Samson called out to the Lord, begging God to remember him and grant him strength one final time. He asked for the power to take vengeance on his enemies for the loss of his sight. Even in his personal pain, his prayer showed renewed faith in God as the true source of all power.

Samson placed his right hand against one central pillar and his left hand against the other. These two middle columns held up the main beams of the entire temple structure. By bracing himself against them, he prepared for his final act of strength.

differ.view: Some say it was a kind of suicide, even though his goal was to kill Israel's enemies. The Bible does not praise that part of his act, and Samson is a tragic hero of faith.

notes.meaning: Samson cried out, asking to die alongside the Philistines, and pushed the pillars with all his might. The building gave way and crashed down on the rulers and the thousands of people gathered inside and on the roof. In his death, Samson struck a heavier blow against the enemies of Israel than during his entire lifetime.

notes.meaning: Samson's family traveled down to Gaza to retrieve his body, and the terrified Philistines did not stop them. They buried him in the family tomb between Zorah and Eshtaol, recording that he had judged Israel for twenty years. His life ended in personal tragedy, yet God used him to begin breaking the power of the Philistines.
